skill: Visual acuity / habitual glasses and pinhole
context: Original Monash 2024–2025 review-inspired final-year decision
stem: A 29-year-old woman attends after gardening with a gritty right eye. She usually wears spectacles for distance. With spectacles, acuity is 6/12 in each eye; each eye improves to 6/6 with pinhole. Her pupil reactions and visual fields are normal. A student says her glasses should have been removed for the first chart reading.
ask: Which statement about the initial acuity assessment is correct?
options: Testing with habitual spectacles was appropriate and the correction should be documented.
Improvement with pinhole proves that no corneal abrasion or foreign body is present.
Bilateral 6/12 acuity confirms that this right-eye injury has reduced her vision.
A result of 6/12 means that she sees twice as far as someone with 6/6.
Routine acuity testing must always be performed first with prescription glasses removed.
explanations: Correct. Test and record each eye with its normal correction; pinhole helps estimate how much reduced acuity is explained by refractive error.
Pinhole improvement does not inspect the corneal surface. Fluorescein examination and lid eversion may still be needed.
Similar bilateral acuity with improvement through pinhole is not evidence of an injury-induced unilateral deficit.
The interpretation is reversed: at six metres she sees what a person with standard vision sees at twelve metres.
Unaided acuity may also be documented, but habitual corrected acuity is a clinically useful initial measurement.
pearl: Always record whether acuity is corrected, unaided or pinhole; examine each eye separately.
pivot: Sudden unilateral acuity loss, severe pain or photophobia requires urgent ophthalmic assessment even if pinhole helps.

steps: Recognise
Ask about mechanism, contact lenses and visual symptoms.
Assess
Record each eye's acuity with correction and pinhole.
Treat
Assess cornea, pupil, lid and fluorescein findings.
Follow up
Treat and refer according to ocular red flags.
management.safety: A better pinhole result does not exclude a painful retained foreign body.
management.local: Australian clinical practice: apply local policy and senior advice.

skill: Skin graft / large defect and contraction
context: Original Monash 2024–2025 review-inspired final-year decision
stem: A road-trauma patient has a clean vascularised 18-by-14-cm soft-tissue defect over the lateral thigh. Direct closure would place excessive tension on the remaining skin. The surgical team discusses harvesting either a split-thickness graft or a full-thickness graft from a donor site.
ask: Which characteristic favours the split-thickness graft here?
options: It routinely provides a closer cosmetic match than a thicker skin graft.
It can be meshed and expanded to cover relatively large wound surfaces.
It produces the least contraction of all skin-graft types during healing.
It is always more durable under repeated daily friction after incorporation.
It has higher oxygen demands than a full-thickness graft during initial take.
explanations: Full-thickness grafts often give better cosmetic match and less contraction, though results depend on the wound and site.
Correct. Split-thickness grafts cover large defects more efficiently and can be meshed, making limited donor skin go further.
Split-thickness grafts are more likely to contract secondarily; rehabilitation and joint positioning may be important.
These thinner grafts can be more fragile than thicker skin and are not automatically more trauma-resistant.
A thinner graft generally takes more reliably on a suitable bed than a more metabolically demanding full-thickness graft.
pearl: Split-thickness for extensive coverage; full-thickness may offer better cosmesis and reduced late contraction.
pivot: Exposed unvascularised tendon or bone may require a flap or wound-bed preparation rather than a simple graft.

steps: Recognise
Assess depth, infection and vascularity of the wound bed.
Assess
Discuss donor-site availability and functional site risks.
Treat
Secure the graft after debridement and coverage planning.
Follow up
Monitor take, dressings and rehabilitation to limit contracture.
management.safety: Do not graft onto avascular tissue without appropriate reconstructive planning.
management.local: Australian clinical practice: apply local policy and senior advice.

context: Original Monash 2024–2025 review-inspired final-year decision
stem: A worker arrives pale and clammy with active spurting blood from a deep forearm laceration. The towel covering the wound has become saturated and his radial pulse is weak. Before anyone has obtained blood samples, an intern asks whether they should first secure IV access or measure blood pressure.
ask: What is the single most urgent action?
options: Measure a complete set of observations before disturbing the wound covering.
Take crossmatch blood immediately while continuing to observe the blood loss.
Apply firm direct pressure over the bleeding source and summon resuscitation help.
Give intravenous opioid analgesia before manipulating the painful wound.
Request vascular ultrasound to identify the damaged artery prior to compression.
explanations: Observations quantify severity but cannot replace immediate control of visible catastrophic bleeding.
Crossmatching is vital to transfusion planning, but it can occur alongside haemorrhage control rather than delaying it.
Correct. Direct pressure is fast and lifesaving; an appropriate tourniquet may follow if limb haemorrhage remains uncontrolled.
Analgesia improves comfort but does not stop exsanguination and should follow immediate haemorrhage control.
Imaging may guide later repair but is not necessary to start compression on an obvious external bleeding site.
pearl: In life-threatening external bleeding, immediate control of haemorrhage comes before routine diagnostic tasks.
pivot: Uncontrolled life-threatening limb bleeding after pressure warrants an arterial tourniquet if available and correctly applied.

steps: Recognise
Recognise catastrophic visible blood loss and activate the trauma team.
Assess
Press firmly on the bleeding wound with suitable protection.
Treat
Establish access and initiate blood-product resuscitation.
Follow up
Arrange definitive surgical haemostasis and perfusion checks.
management.safety: Do not delay pressure while waiting for tests or repeatedly lifting the dressing.
management.local: Australian clinical practice: apply local policy and senior advice.

skill: Major GI haemorrhage / wide peripheral access
context: Original Monash 2024–2025 review-inspired final-year decision
stem: A 58-year-old with severe haematemesis is hypotensive at 83/46 mmHg and tachycardic at 132/min. Two antecubital veins are accessible. One junior proposes a standard triple-lumen central line as the fastest route for urgent packed red blood cell transfusion.
ask: Which access should be established first?
options: A single 22-gauge hand cannula with an infusion pump attached.
A routine triple-lumen neck central catheter as sole vascular access.
A pair of small hand cannulas used together to reduce puncture size.
Two short, large-bore peripheral cannulas allowing rapid blood delivery.
No cannula until the cause of bleeding is confirmed by endoscopy.
explanations: A narrow cannula limits rapid volume delivery and does not give access redundancy.
A standard triple lumen is long and relatively narrow, often offering less rapid flow than a short wide peripheral catheter.
Two very small cannulas may still be insufficient during major haemorrhage when large peripheral veins are available.
Correct. Two wide short peripheral IV cannulas offer high flow and redundancy; commonly use 14–16G when safely possible.
Endoscopy may stop the bleeding but resuscitation cannot wait until diagnostic or therapeutic procedures begin.
pearl: Short, wide peripheral IV access can outperform ordinary multilumen central access for rapid transfusion.
pivot: When large peripheral veins cannot be accessed, seek IO or specialist rapid-infusion access.

steps: Recognise
Recognise shock and activate a major haemorrhage protocol.
Assess
Establish two wide IVs and obtain key blood tests.
Treat
Begin blood products and monitor perfusion and haemodynamics.
Follow up
Arrange urgent definitive bleeding control and reassess volume status.
management.safety: Central venous catheters are not automatically the highest-flow resuscitation access.
management.local: Australian clinical practice: apply local policy and senior advice.

skill: Upper airway obstruction / jaw thrust before tests
context: Original Monash 2024–2025 review-inspired final-year decision
stem: Thirty minutes after surgery, a sedated patient becomes difficult to rouse, develops noisy inspiratory breathing and has visibly inadequate chest movement. Cyanosis is developing. Emergency help has been summoned. A colleague wants to take an arterial blood gas before deciding whether to intervene.
ask: What immediate bedside intervention is best?
options: Obtain a blood gas to determine whether there is carbon dioxide retention.
Give an intravenous sedative to suppress distress and reduce breathing effort.
Transfer for urgent neck imaging before attempting basic airway manoeuvres.
Apply a chest monitor and defer manoeuvres until a full observation set returns.
Open the airway with jaw thrust and assist oxygenation and ventilation as needed.
explanations: Blood gas analysis may help later but must not delay the restoration of airflow.
Additional sedation can worsen upper-airway obstruction, reduce protective reflexes and suppress respiratory drive.
Imaging is unsafe as the initial plan when ventilation is ineffective; the airway must be managed clinically.
Monitoring is useful while resuscitating but does not replace manoeuvres that reopen the airway.
Correct. Jaw thrust can relieve soft-tissue obstruction rapidly, followed by appropriate suction, oxygen, bag-mask ventilation and experienced airway assistance.
pearl: Call for help, open the obstructed airway and ventilate; investigation comes after oxygenation.
pivot: Persistent stridor despite positioning may be laryngospasm or swelling requiring anaesthetic expertise.

steps: Recognise
Recognise obstructed respiration and confirm emergency activation.
Assess
Open the airway using jaw thrust and positioning.
Treat
Use bag-mask ventilation with oxygen when required.
Follow up
Escalate for an advanced airway if obstruction persists.
management.safety: A jaw thrust does not reliably relieve true laryngeal oedema or laryngospasm.
management.local: Australian clinical practice: apply local policy and senior advice.

context: Original Monash 2024–2025 review-inspired final-year question
stem: A 20-year-old with type 1 diabetes reports that her insulin-pump tubing came loose overnight. This morning she has abdominal pain, vomiting and deep breathing; her glucose is 24 mmol/L and she is dehydrated. A trainee requests HbA1c and fasting glucose but has not yet checked blood ketones.
ask: Which combination most directly confirms the time-critical diagnosis?
options: Venous gas to assess acidosis and bedside blood beta-hydroxybutyrate to assess ketosis.
A glycated haemoglobin result and a fasting glucose reading taken once nausea resolves.
Urine glucose dipstick and a nonurgent serum C-peptide concentration.
Microalbuminuria screen and fasting lipid profile after intravenous hydration.
Serum insulin assay and plasma osmolality alone before ketone assessment.
explanations: Correct. DKA is a triad of hyperglycaemia, ketonaemia and acidosis; blood ketones plus venous gas rapidly establish the mechanism.
HbA1c assesses chronic glycaemic exposure, not acute acid-base severity. Waiting for fasting glucose delays resuscitation.
Glycosuria is nonspecific; C-peptide is unnecessary to diagnose DKA in someone known to have type 1 diabetes.
Albuminuria and lipids assess chronic risk, not the acute metabolic emergency.
Insulin concentration does not substitute for blood ketones; osmolality is relevant to dehydration and HHS but insufficient to identify DKA.
pearl: Pump users have no long-acting insulin depot; line interruption can cause DKA rapidly.
pivot: A patient receiving SGLT2 inhibitors can develop ketoacidosis even without marked hyperglycaemia.

steps: Recognise
Assess airway, breathing, circulation and volume depletion.
Investigate
Check blood ketones, VBG, electrolytes and renal function.
Treat
Begin local DKA IV fluid/insulin protocol after checking potassium.
Follow up
Identify pump fault and arrange diabetes-team review before safe discharge.
management.safety: Never delay suspected DKA treatment while waiting for HbA1c or urine ketones.
management.local: Use current Australian and local hospital clinical practice.

skill: Fever after splenectomy / overwhelming sepsis risk
context: Original Monash 2024–2025 review-inspired final-year question
stem: An 11-year-old who had a splenectomy after trauma presents with temperature 38.9°C and mild sore throat. He has not completed his pneumococcal boosters. He is currently talking normally and has normal capillary refill. His parent wonders whether he could take paracetamol and return if the fever lasts three days.
ask: What is the safest response?
options: Treat presumed viral illness symptomatically because the child's perfusion is currently normal.
Arrange urgent medical assessment and early empirical antibiotics for possible overwhelming infection.
Wait for a positive throat or blood culture before considering treatment with antibiotics.
Offer catch-up vaccination without additional assessment because this prevents acute bacterial sepsis.
Observe overnight at home so that fever patterns can help distinguish viral from bacterial illness.
explanations: Well appearance early in an illness does not exclude rapidly progressive postsplenectomy bacterial sepsis.
Correct. Asplenia increases susceptibility to life-threatening encapsulated bacterial infection; fever is an emergency even if focal signs are few.
Cultures should be taken promptly where possible, but waiting for positivity could allow fulminant infection to progress.
Vaccination is essential prevention but cannot protect the child from a current invasive infection once symptoms begin.
Home observation risks delayed presentation after deterioration. Emergency evaluation and antibiotic treatment are time-sensitive.
pearl: Fever in a person without a spleen deserves urgent evaluation and antibiotics, even before severe signs appear.
pivot: When recovered, review vaccinations, prophylactic antibiotics and the family's written emergency fever plan.

steps: Recognise
Identify postsplenectomy risk and assess sepsis observations.
Investigate
Obtain cultures and basic bloods without delaying treatment.
Treat
Administer empirical antibiotics according to local paediatric sepsis protocol.
Follow up
Reassess immunisation records and provide ongoing fever-action advice.
management.safety: Do not wait for meningism, rash or shock in a febrile asplenic child.
management.local: Use current Australian and local hospital clinical practice.

skill: Pulseless electrical activity / appropriate ALS medication
context: Original Monash 2024–2025 review-inspired final-year question
stem: Staff find a 70-year-old unresponsive and apnoeic. The monitor shows an organised narrow-complex rhythm at 32 beats/min, but a prompt central pulse check detects no pulse. CPR begins. One clinician suggests atropine because the displayed ventricular rate is very slow.
ask: Which drug belongs in the immediate arrest pathway?
options: Atropine 600 micrograms IV because the electrical rhythm is bradycardic.
Amiodarone 300 mg IV because all pulseless rhythms are shockable.
Adrenaline 1 mg IV or IO during CPR, while investigating reversible causes.
Adenosine 6 mg IV because the visible QRS complexes are narrow.
Metoprolol 5 mg IV because the conduction pattern remains organised.
explanations: Atropine may be used for symptomatic bradycardia with a pulse; it is not a routine treatment for PEA arrest.
Amiodarone is used for selected refractory shockable arrest rhythms, not for PEA.
Correct. No mechanical output despite electrical activity defines PEA; CPR, adrenaline and reversible-cause treatment are indicated, not defibrillation.
Adenosine targets particular tachycardias with a pulse. It cannot restore output in a pulseless slow rhythm.
Beta-blockade may further reduce cardiac output and has no role in the initial non-shockable ALS pathway.
pearl: Distinguish a slow rhythm with a pulse from PEA: the latter is cardiac arrest.
pivot: VF or pulseless VT calls for unsynchronised defibrillation; PEA does not.

steps: Recognise
Confirm unresponsiveness, abnormal breathing and absent pulse.
Investigate
Initiate CPR, monitor rhythm and assess reversible Hs and Ts.
Treat
Give IV/IO adrenaline on the current ANZCOR non-shockable pathway.
Follow up
Continue cycles and document reversible cause and response.
management.safety: Do not shock an organised pulseless rhythm simply because the patient is in arrest.
management.local: Use current Australian and local hospital clinical practice.

skill: Left ventricular failure after MI / cardiorenal deterioration
context: Original Monash 2024–2025 review-inspired final-year question
stem: A 63-year-old develops orthopnoea and oliguria one day after a large anterior STEMI. Examination reveals an elevated JVP, bilateral crackles and cool extremities. Radiography shows symmetrical perihilar pulmonary oedema, and creatinine has risen despite no substantial fluid administration.
ask: Which explanation best connects the clinical abnormalities?
options: New aspiration pneumonia is responsible for both the wet lungs and kidney failure.
Simple dehydration is reducing renal flow and causing diffuse pulmonary opacification.
Primary glomerulonephritis is causing pulmonary oedema independently of the infarction.
Acute left ventricular pump dysfunction causes congestion and impaired renal perfusion.
An isolated right-sided pleural effusion has precipitated all systemic findings.
explanations: Aspiration may complicate admission but the heart-failure findings and MI chronology provide a more cohesive explanation.
Dehydration does not easily explain raised JVP and pulmonary congestion; large fluids risk worsening respiratory failure.
Glomerulonephritis is not suggested by the chronology or other findings and is a less direct cause.
Correct. Poor LV function raises pulmonary venous pressures and lowers forward flow, causing pulmonary oedema and cardiorenal dysfunction.
An isolated pleural effusion does not produce this widespread pulmonary congestion and post-MI low-output pattern.
pearl: Acute cardiac decompensation can reduce kidney filtration while total body fluid is elevated.
pivot: An increase in creatinine with raised JVP is not automatically an indication for additional IV crystalloid.

steps: Recognise
Assess ABC, oxygenation, BP and shock signs.
Investigate
Use ECG, bedside echo, fluid balance and serial kidney tests.
Treat
Give cardiology-directed treatment of pulmonary congestion and poor perfusion.
Follow up
Monitor urine output, electrolytes and need for intensive care.
management.safety: Indiscriminate crystalloid resuscitation can worsen cardiogenic pulmonary oedema.
management.local: Use current Australian and local hospital clinical practice.

skill: Severe asthma / normalising CO2 and ventilatory failure
context: Original Monash 2024–2025 review-inspired final-year question
stem: A 27-year-old with acute asthma has received repeated salbutamol, ipratropium, systemic steroids and magnesium. She now speaks only in words, has a near-silent chest, and is progressively tired. Saturation is 96% with oxygen via mask. Arterial gas shows pH 7.27 and PaCO2 49 mmHg.
ask: What does the blood gas indicate in context?
options: The normal oxygen saturation excludes an impending respiratory arrest.
Bronchodilators have improved ventilation because PaCO2 has risen towards normal.
The measured acidaemia is purely metabolic and unrelated to asthma severity.
Stable carbon dioxide during severe bronchospasm is an expected reassuring finding.
The patient is developing ventilatory failure and needs immediate senior airway assistance.
explanations: Supplemental oxygen can maintain saturation even while ventilation is failing and carbon dioxide is accumulating.
In early asthma the patient often hyperventilates and CO2 falls; a rise despite persistent distress is concerning for exhaustion.
The increased PaCO2 with reduced pH signifies respiratory acidosis, not isolated metabolic pathology.
A normal or raised PaCO2 in an exhausted asthmatic is ominous, particularly with reduced air movement.
Correct. Rising CO2, acidemia, exhaustion and a silent chest are signs of impending respiratory arrest; call ICU/anaesthesia immediately while continuing treatment.
pearl: Beware a ‘normal’ CO2 in life-threatening asthma: fatigue may be replacing earlier hyperventilation.
pivot: A truly improving patient has reduced work of breathing and better air entry, not exhaustion.

steps: Recognise
Activate rapid resuscitation and expert airway help.
Investigate
Continue monitored oxygen, bronchodilators and systemic therapies.
Treat
Prepare controlled ventilation only with experienced airway support.
Follow up
Track clinical effort, gases and complications after stabilisation.
management.safety: Intubation in severe asthma can cause dynamic hyperinflation and must be performed by skilled teams.
management.local: Use current Australian and local hospital clinical practice.

skill: PE after admission / high pretest probability
context: New original clinical cases inspired by 2024–2025 Monash SPA-W reviews
stem: A 67-year-old with COPD is brought in after sudden pleuritic chest pain and unexplained hypoxia. He was discharged from hospital last week after an infective admission. Temperature is normal, WCC and CRP are not elevated, and lung auscultation is comparatively clear. A bedside radiograph reveals no sizeable infiltrate or effusion.
ask: Which diagnosis is most important to investigate promptly?
options: Acute pulmonary embolism related to recent hospitalisation and immobility.
Uncomplicated right-sided pneumonia despite no inflammatory or radiographic changes.
Large pleural effusion despite normal percussion and no visible fluid collection.
Simple COPD exacerbation despite absent wheeze and sudden pleuritic pain.
Uncomplicated costochondritis despite objective hypoxaemia and recent admission.
explanations: Correct. Recent immobility and abrupt pleuritic pain with hypoxia and relatively clear lungs raise PE probability; assess haemodynamic risk and obtain appropriate definitive imaging.
Pneumonia can sometimes have atypical findings, but the sudden onset and lack of infection markers make it less compelling here.
A significant pleural effusion commonly gives dullness and fluid on imaging; the stated findings make it less likely.
COPD can cause hypoxia but does not fully explain sudden focal pleuritic pain, recent admission and absence of an obvious exacerbation pattern.
Costochondritis can cause reproducible pain, but should not explain hypoxaemia; serious cardiopulmonary causes need exclusion.
pearl: Think PE when disproportionate hypoxia or pleuritic pain occurs with relatively clear lung examination.
pivot: High clinical probability leads to imaging; D-dimer alone cannot rule out PE in high-risk patients.

steps: Recognise
Assess vitals, oxygen requirement, clinical PE probability and shock.
Assess
Investigate with CTPA or appropriate alternative; assess renal and contrast risks.
Treat
Start anticoagulation when indicated after bleeding risk review and diagnostic pathway.
Reassess
Check RV strain and plan admission, treatment duration and provoking risks.
management.safety: Normal oxygen saturation or a benign chest examination does not safely rule out PE.
management.local: Use current Australian guidelines and local hospital policy.

skill: Denosumab hypocalcaemia / CKD and bone turnover
context: New original clinical cases inspired by 2024–2025 Monash SPA-W reviews
stem: A 79-year-old treated for osteoporosis presents with circumoral tingling and painful hand spasms ten days after an injection. She has stage 4 CKD. Calcium is 1.78 mmol/L and magnesium is mildly reduced; potassium is normal. Her medicines include perindopril, an SGLT2 inhibitor, metformin and six-monthly denosumab.
ask: Which medicine is the most likely contributor?
options: Perindopril through angiotensin-converting-enzyme inhibition and altered renal potassium excretion.
Denosumab through reduced osteoclastic calcium release, particularly in chronic kidney disease.
Metformin through impaired vitamin absorption causing isolated acute severe hypocalcaemia.
Empagliflozin through urinary glucose excretion and acute direct loss of serum calcium.
A standard low-dose paracetamol regimen through reduced intestinal calcium absorption.
explanations: Perindopril can raise potassium or creatinine but is not the main recognised cause of profound hypocalcaemia after an injection.
Correct. RANKL inhibition suppresses osteoclast-mediated bone resorption; advanced CKD increases susceptibility to serious denosumab-associated hypocalcaemia.
Long-term metformin is associated with vitamin B12 issues, not a characteristic acute calcium drop with tetany.
SGLT2 inhibitors influence volume and metabolic outcomes, but the timing and calcium physiology most strongly implicate denosumab.
Paracetamol is not a usual cause of acute symptomatic hypocalcaemia; looking for a time-related medication effect is more informative.
pearl: Denosumab can cause dangerous hypocalcaemia, especially in CKD; monitor calcium and vitamin D status.
pivot: Symptomatic tetany or arrhythmia from hypocalcaemia may require monitored IV calcium and senior input.

steps: Recognise
Recognise symptomatic low calcium and assess ECG/QT changes.
Assess
Check corrected or ionised calcium, magnesium, phosphate, vitamin D and kidney function.
Treat
Provide calcium replacement appropriate to severity, with ECG monitoring if needed.
Reassess
Review denosumab suitability and preventive supplementation before future doses.
management.safety: Correct magnesium deficiency where present and avoid assuming paresthesia is benign anxiety.
management.local: Use current Australian guidelines and local hospital policy.

context: New original clinical cases inspired by 2024–2025 Monash SPA-W reviews
stem: A 41-year-old underwent laparoscopic upper abdominal surgery yesterday. She now has worsening diffuse pain and a progressively firm, tender swelling near the operative site. She is pale, pulse is 114/min and haemoglobin has fallen from 138 g/L before surgery to 101 g/L. Oxygenation remains normal and she has no fever.
ask: Which response most safely addresses the likely complication?
options: Order routine bowel aperients to relieve discomfort from postoperative constipation.
Treat pain with extra opioids and schedule routine surgical review tomorrow.
Escalate immediately for suspected operative bleeding and possible urgent re-exploration.
Arrange an erect chest radiograph first to quantify expected postoperative free gas.
Provide a diet trial and observe because postoperative pain is expected after laparoscopy.
explanations: Aperients would not treat a substantial fall in haemoglobin or enlarging tender mass and may distract from haemorrhage.
Pain relief is appropriate concurrently, but worsening pain plus pallor and falling haemoglobin demand immediate surgical assessment.

Correct. A large haemoglobin drop with worsening pain and focal swelling raises concern for internal bleeding or haematoma; resuscitate and obtain urgent senior surgical decisions on imaging versus theatre.
Some free gas may persist after laparoscopy but cannot explain the full haemodynamic and haematological picture; radiography should not postpone escalation.
Postoperative soreness is common, but escalating pain with blood loss is not reassuring. Oral intake may be unsafe if urgent theatre is required.
pearl: An otherwise normal SpO₂ does not exclude postoperative blood loss.
pivot: Operative re-exploration timing is a senior surgical decision; instability may require immediate theatre without further scans.

steps: Recognise
Review shock signs, abdominal examination and operative documentation.
Assess
Repeat FBC, crossmatch, coagulation and bedside imaging if appropriate.
Treat
Resuscitate and contact the responsible surgeon urgently about source control.
Reassess
Monitor observations and haemoglobin and prepare for definitive treatment.
management.safety: Do not label progressive postoperative pain with significant haemoglobin fall as routine ileus.
management.local: Use current Australian guidelines and local hospital policy.

context: New original clinical cases inspired by 2024–2025 Monash SPA-W reviews
stem: A validated diagnostic test used in a study has 80% sensitivity and 100% specificity, with a clearly defined population and no observed false positives. A clinician argues that the negative results are therefore more reliable than positive results for excluding disease. Assume these performance characteristics are exact in the question.
ask: Which inference is correct under those idealised assumptions?
options: Twenty per cent of unaffected people receive false-positive results from this assay.
The assay can rule out the condition reliably because sensitivity approaches perfection.
A negative test completely excludes the condition because specificity reaches one hundred per cent.
A positive result rules in the condition because the test produces no false positives.
The predictive value of a positive test must equal the disease prevalence exactly.
explanations: An 80% sensitivity is the true-positive rate; specificity of 100% means the false-positive rate is zero, not 20%.
Sensitivity of 80% leaves false negatives, so a negative cannot reliably exclude disease.
Specificity addresses people without disease, not the false negatives among affected patients.
Correct. If specificity truly equals 100%, no unaffected patient tests positive; a positive result must be a true positive in the idealised model.
Positive predictive value depends on prevalence as well as test characteristics; with zero false positives, PPV is ideally 100% wherever true positives occur.
pearl: SpPin: high SPecificity, positive rules IN; SnNout: high SeNsitivity, negative rules OUT.
pivot: Real studies report estimates with confidence intervals; observed 100% specificity does not guarantee zero false positives in all future settings.

steps: Recognise
Identify sensitivity, specificity and population prevalence.
Assess
Draw a two-by-two table for affected and unaffected groups.
Treat
Calculate test positives and negatives, including false-negative results.
Reassess
Explain the interpretation and limitations of measured performance.
management.safety: Do not treat an estimated 100% specificity from a small sample as infallible in practice.
management.local: Use current Australian guidelines and local hospital policy.

context: New original clinical cases inspired by 2024–2025 Monash SPA-W reviews
stem: A 56-year-old with type 2 diabetes takes metformin, empagliflozin, amlodipine and a proton pump inhibitor. She is scheduled for elective abdominal surgery in four days and asks which regular medicine needs a planned interruption to reduce metabolic complications from fasting and surgical stress.
ask: Which action is most appropriate?
options: Continue every medicine until the operating-table assessment to avoid perioperative hyperglycaemia.
Stop the proton pump inhibitor several days before surgery to reduce aspiration risk.
Stop amlodipine alone for three days because it increases ketone production during fasting.
Stop metformin permanently because all diabetes drugs create the same euglycaemic ketosis risk.
Withhold empagliflozin for the recommended preoperative interval and monitor ketones if unwell.
explanations: SGLT2 inhibitors are associated with perioperative ketoacidosis even when glucose is not markedly high, so universal continuation is unsafe.
A proton pump inhibitor does not confer the specific euglycaemic DKA risk described.
Amlodipine is not an SGLT2 inhibitor and is not the culprit medicine for perioperative euglycaemic ketosis.
Metformin may have separate perioperative considerations, but this question asks about the specific SGLT2-related ketoacidosis risk.
Correct. Australian guidance commonly withholds empagliflozin at least three days inclusive of surgery day (two prior days plus day of surgery); assess ketones and local restart guidance.
pearl: Perioperative SGLT2 inhibitors risk euglycaemic DKA; normal glucose cannot exclude it.
pivot: A symptomatic post-operative patient with nausea, vomiting and acidosis needs ketone/VBG assessment even if bedside glucose is near normal.

steps: Recognise
Review diabetes medicines and planned fasting and operation.
Assess
Plan SGLT2 interruption with the anaesthetic/diabetes team.
Treat
Monitor glycaemia, ketones and clinical status if unwell.
Reassess
Restart when eating, drinking and metabolically stable per local plan.
management.safety: Do not restart an SGLT2 inhibitor while fasting or during unresolved ketoacidosis risk.
management.local: Use current Australian guidelines and local hospital policy.

context: Original final-year Monash-style decision; inspired by 2024–2025 SPA-W review themes
stem: A 31-year-old arrives after a high-speed motorcycle collision. He is agitated, severely hypoxic and hypotensive at 72/42 mmHg. The left hemithorax barely moves, breath sounds are absent on that side and his neck veins are prominent. A portable radiograph has been ordered but has not arrived.
ask: What should the resuscitation team prioritise immediately?
options: Perform emergency left chest decompression by a trained clinician without waiting for imaging.
Obtain a portable chest radiograph to confirm the suspected unilateral pleural air.
Send urgent arterial blood gases before undertaking a potentially invasive chest procedure.
Start non-invasive positive-pressure ventilation while waiting for formal thoracic ultrasound.
Transport for contrast-enhanced chest CT to identify associated vascular and lung injuries.
explanations: Correct. Clinical tension pneumothorax with shock requires immediate decompression; finger thoracostomy or needle decompression according to expertise and trauma protocol, followed by definitive drainage.
A radiograph can diagnose a stable pneumothorax, but waiting in obstructive shock may cause cardiac arrest.
ABG can quantify respiratory failure but adds no information needed before lifesaving decompression.
Positive-pressure ventilation without relieving pleural tension can worsen haemodynamic collapse and should not delay decompression.
CT is appropriate only after stabilisation and would be unsafe during untreated tension physiology.
pearl: Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis in an unstable trauma patient; treat before imaging.
pivot: A stable patient with unilateral chest pain and preserved circulation can undergo bedside ultrasound or radiography first.

steps: Recognise
Identify unilateral absent air entry, severe hypoxia and obstructive shock.
Assess
Call trauma support and assess for concurrent haemorrhage or airway compromise.
Act
Decompress the affected chest immediately using a trained clinician and local technique.
Reassess
Arrange definitive pleural drainage, monitor response and reassess for other injuries.
management.safety: Do not delay decompression for X-ray or CT when clinical tension pneumothorax causes shock.
management.local: Use current Australian clinical guidance, local protocols and senior support.

context: Original final-year Monash-style decision; inspired by 2024–2025 SPA-W review themes
stem: A 59-year-old receiving cytotoxic chemotherapy for lymphoma presents with rigors, temperature 39.1°C, pulse 126/min and BP 89/55 mmHg. Her last blood count showed severe neutropenia. Blood cultures have been drawn; the new full blood count and chest radiograph are pending. A junior wants to await the neutrophil result before prescribing treatment.
ask: What is the most appropriate next action?
options: Wait for the absolute neutrophil count to confirm the precise severity of neutropenia.
Begin empirical broad-spectrum IV antibiotics immediately while resuscitating suspected sepsis.
Obtain a chest CT to locate an infectious focus before choosing antibiotic therapy.
Give oral antibiotics and arrange outpatient review if the fever decreases after paracetamol.
Administer granulocyte colony-stimulating factor alone while monitoring for spontaneous improvement.
explanations: The clinical context already indicates a high-risk immunocompromised patient; a repeat count should not postpone treatment.
Correct. Febrile neutropenia with hypotension is a time-critical sepsis emergency. Obtain cultures without delaying antibiotics and start appropriate IV antipseudomonal therapy promptly.
Imaging can identify a source later but must not postpone first-dose antibiotics in shock.
Hypotension makes outpatient oral management inappropriate regardless of transient temperature reduction.
G-CSF has selected indications but cannot replace immediate infection treatment or shock resuscitation.
pearl: Treat fever after cytotoxic chemotherapy as neutropenic sepsis until assessed; never wait for the repeat ANC.
pivot: Stable low-risk febrile neutropenia can follow a risk-stratified pathway, but systemic compromise mandates urgent IV therapy.

steps: Recognise
Recognise immunocompromise, fever and haemodynamic compromise.
Assess
Obtain cultures and lactate promptly without delaying treatment.
Act
Give immediate broad-spectrum IV antibiotics and guided sepsis resuscitation.
Reassess
Reassess perfusion, culture results, source control and escalation to critical care.
management.safety: Time to antibiotics matters: current eviQ recommends within one hour for neutropenic sepsis or septic shock.
management.local: Use current Australian clinical guidance, local protocols and senior support.

skill: Metastatic spinal cord compression / urgent MRI and steroids
context: Original final-year Monash-style decision; inspired by 2024–2025 SPA-W review themes
stem: A 66-year-old with metastatic prostate cancer reports new thoracic back pain, progressive bilateral leg weakness and difficulty starting urination. Examination shows brisk knee reflexes and reduced sensation below the umbilicus. His observations are stable, and plain spinal radiographs show degenerative changes without an acute fracture.
ask: What management best preserves neurological function?
options: Arrange routine outpatient physiotherapy and review weakness after two weeks of rehabilitation.
Request an isolated lumbar X-ray and provide analgesia while awaiting the radiology report.
Start dexamethasone promptly and organise urgent whole-spine MRI with specialist assessment.
Order an elective nerve-conduction study to distinguish neuropathy from spinal root irritation.
Prescribe oral opioids alone because stable vital signs make neurological compression unlikely.
explanations: New weakness and bladder dysfunction in cancer are red flags for cord compression, not a routine rehabilitation referral.
Plain radiographs cannot exclude epidural tumour or compression and delay definitive MRI.
Correct. Suspected malignant spinal cord compression warrants prompt dexamethasone, urgent whole-spine MRI and coordinated oncology/spinal surgical assessment.
Electrophysiology is not the first investigation for acute upper motor neurone signs and sphincter dysfunction.
Analgesia is appropriate but does not address the risk of irreversible cord injury despite stable vital signs.
pearl: Back pain plus new motor or sphincter symptoms in metastatic cancer is spinal cord compression until excluded.
pivot: Even if pain is mild, objective upper motor neurone signs and urinary symptoms justify emergency MRI.

steps: Recognise
Document motor power, sensory level, gait and bladder function.
Assess
Request urgent whole-spine MRI and involve oncology and spinal surgery.
Act
Give prompt dexamethasone according to protocol while arranging decompression or radiotherapy.
Reassess
Protect spinal stability, monitor neurological changes and manage steroid complications.
management.safety: Do not delay treatment because a plain X-ray is normal; permanent paraplegia may follow delay.
management.local: Use current Australian clinical guidance, local protocols and senior support.

context: Original final-year Monash-style decision; inspired by 2024–2025 SPA-W review themes
stem: A previously healthy five-year-old has refused to bear weight since waking, with fever 39°C and severe right groin pain. The hip rests flexed and externally rotated, and passive rotation causes marked distress. CRP is elevated and ultrasound shows a substantial hip effusion; there is no history of injury.
ask: What is the safest next step?
options: Arrange discharge with oral analgesia and a review appointment after the weekend.
Start physiotherapy immediately to prevent reduced hip range from immobility.
Treat presumed transient synovitis with ibuprofen and reassess in one week.
Seek urgent orthopaedic review for aspiration or washout and commence IV antibiotics.
Obtain an elective MRI before contacting orthopaedics or administering any antimicrobial therapy.
explanations: A febrile child unable to bear weight with a painful effusion may have septic arthritis requiring urgent intervention.
Physiotherapy is not the priority during suspected infection and may increase pain.
Transient synovitis is a differential but severe fever, inflammatory markers and inability to bear weight warrant infection exclusion.
Correct. Septic arthritis threatens cartilage; urgent orthopaedic aspiration or washout and IV antibiotics are indicated, without delaying treatment in an unwell child.
MRI can assess adjacent osteomyelitis but should not delay urgent surgical discussion or antibiotic treatment.
pearl: Hot, painful immobile hip with fever in a child is septic arthritis until proven otherwise.
pivot: A well child walking comfortably with a small effusion and no systemic features may be assessed for transient synovitis.

steps: Recognise
Assess for sepsis, pain, limb perfusion and weight-bearing ability.
Assess
Obtain blood cultures, inflammatory markers and urgent orthopaedic assessment.
Act
Give IV antibiotics per local protocol and arrange joint aspiration or washout.
Reassess
Monitor fever, inflammatory markers and return of joint movement with the team.
management.safety: Never delay antibiotics in a systemically unwell child while waiting for MRI or joint aspiration.
management.local: Use current Australian clinical guidance, local protocols and senior support.

skill: Infected obstructed ureter / urgent source control
context: Original final-year Monash-style decision; inspired by 2024–2025 SPA-W review themes
stem: A 44-year-old presents with severe left loin pain, shaking chills and vomiting. Temperature is 39.4°C, BP 90/58 mmHg and creatinine is rising. CT reveals an 8-mm proximal ureteric calculus with upstream hydronephrosis and inflammatory stranding. The urine dipstick is positive for nitrites and leukocytes.
ask: Which intervention is essential alongside resuscitation and IV antibiotics?
options: Arrange routine outpatient ureteroscopy after several days of oral antibiotic therapy.
Begin medical expulsive therapy and discharge once the pain improves with analgesia.
Give aggressive intravenous fluids alone because relieving obstruction can be deferred.
Perform immediate definitive stone fragmentation without first treating the septic physiology.
Obtain urgent urological drainage by ureteric stent or percutaneous nephrostomy.
explanations: Infected obstruction with shock needs urgent decompression; outpatient waiting risks uncontrolled sepsis.
Medical expulsive therapy is not definitive source control for an obstructed infected collecting system.
Fluids are necessary for shock but cannot drain infected urine trapped above the stone.
Definitive lithotripsy is generally delayed until infection is controlled; emergency drainage is the first procedural goal.
Correct. An infected obstructed kidney is a urological emergency requiring prompt decompression plus sepsis management, with definitive stone removal later.
pearl: Obstructed infected urinary tract = antibiotics plus drainage; antibiotics alone may fail without source control.
pivot: A noninfected uncomplicated small stone in a stable patient can sometimes be managed expectantly.

steps: Recognise
Identify obstructive urosepsis and activate sepsis resuscitation.
Assess
Obtain cultures, renal tests and urgent imaging or review existing CT.
Act
Give prompt IV antibiotics and coordinate emergency ureteric stent or nephrostomy.
Reassess
Monitor urine output, renal function and haemodynamics; plan later stone clearance.
management.safety: Do not wait for blood culture results or successful pain control before requesting urological decompression.
management.local: Use current Australian clinical guidance, local protocols and senior support.

context: Original final-year Monash-style decision; inspired by 2024–2025 SPA-W review themes
stem: Minutes after receiving IV cefazolin, a 42-year-old develops sudden wheeze, hoarse voice and dizziness. BP falls to 75/40 mmHg and the lips appear swollen. There is no visible urticaria. A colleague suggests giving an antihistamine first because the skin is clear and anaphylaxis has not been confirmed.
ask: What is the correct immediate medication?
options: Give intramuscular adrenaline into the lateral thigh immediately, with resuscitation support.
Give intravenous chlorphenamine first and observe whether the wheeze settles.
Give oral prednisolone first to prevent rapid progression of airway swelling.
Give nebulised salbutamol alone because the most prominent symptom is wheeze.
Give intramuscular glucagon routinely as the first-line drug for all suspected reactions.
explanations: Correct. Airway, breathing and circulatory compromise after exposure is anaphylaxis even without rash; IM adrenaline is first line, with positioning, oxygen and fluids as required.
Antihistamines treat itch and hives but do not reverse shock or critical airway compromise.
Steroids have delayed effects and do not substitute for adrenaline in an acute reaction.
Bronchodilators may supplement adrenaline for persistent wheeze, but cannot reverse systemic vasodilation and airway oedema.
Glucagon may be considered in selected refractory beta-blocker-associated reactions, not as routine initial therapy.
pearl: Anaphylaxis can occur without skin signs; IM adrenaline must not be delayed by antihistamines.
pivot: Persistent shock after appropriate IM adrenaline and fluids requires specialist-led refractory anaphylaxis management.

steps: Recognise
Stop the suspected trigger, call resuscitation and position safely.
Assess
Assess airway swelling, breathing, perfusion and monitoring.
Act
Give IM adrenaline promptly and repeat according to protocol if needed.
Reassess
Provide oxygen, IV fluid for shock, observation and allergy follow-up.
management.safety: Do not allow a hypotensive patient with anaphylaxis to stand or walk; collapse can worsen abruptly.
management.local: Use current Australian clinical guidance, local protocols and senior support.

context: Original final-year Monash-style decision; inspired by 2024–2025 SPA-W review themes
stem: A 73-year-old with severe COPD presents with increased sputum and breathlessness. On room air, SpO₂ is 84%; he is alert and not in shock. After controlled oxygen begins, SpO₂ rises to 97% and he becomes increasingly drowsy. A VBG shows hypercapnia with acidosis. Staff ask what target should be prescribed.
ask: Which oxygen target is generally appropriate during this exacerbation?
options: Aim for 80–84% to avoid any risk of carbon dioxide retention.
Titrate oxygen to 88–92% while assessing ventilation and need for NIV.
Maintain 94–98% because all patients require near-normal oxygen saturation.
Keep saturation above 99% while delivering bronchodilators via oxygen nebuliser.
Stop supplemental oxygen completely until a repeat arterial gas is available.
explanations: This target permits significant hypoxaemia and risks organ injury; controlled oxygen should not mean untreated hypoxia.
Correct. Australian COPD guidance targets 88–92% in most exacerbations, with blood gas assessment and NIV for appropriate hypercapnic acidosis.
Routine high saturation targets can aggravate CO₂ retention in susceptible COPD patients and are not the usual prescribed range.
Maximal oxygen is not routine and oxygen-driven nebulisation may increase CO₂; use air-driven bronchodilator delivery if needed.
Oxygen must not be withheld from hypoxaemic patients; reduce and titrate to the target rather than stopping abruptly.
pearl: Oxygen is a prescribed drug: in acute COPD, target 88–92% unless individualised otherwise.
pivot: A critically hypoxic patient still requires immediate oxygen and resuscitation, not rigid adherence to a target at the expense of survival.

steps: Recognise
Recognise COPD exacerbation, hypoxaemia and altered mental state.
Assess
Check blood gases and assess for hypercapnic respiratory acidosis.
Act
Titrate controlled oxygen to 88–92% and treat exacerbation; consider NIV.
Reassess
Repeat gas and observations and escalate if acidosis or consciousness worsens.
management.safety: Do not withhold oxygen in severe hypoxaemia; excessive oxygen and insufficient oxygen are both dangerous.
management.local: Use current Australian clinical guidance, local protocols and senior support.

skill: Paracetamol overdose / late result start antidote
context: Original final-year Monash-style decision; inspired by 2024–2025 SPA-W review themes
stem: A 22-year-old arrives nine hours after intentionally swallowing approximately 18 g of immediate-release paracetamol. She has nausea but no jaundice. Blood has been drawn for paracetamol concentration and liver tests, yet the regional laboratory cannot provide a result for another three hours. Her weight is 68 kg.
ask: What is the safest next treatment decision?
options: Wait for the serum level because treatment only helps after liver enzymes rise.
Give activated charcoal as the only treatment because absorption is still ongoing.
Start IV acetylcysteine now and revise the plan when results become available.
Give oral vitamin K immediately because it reverses paracetamol-related liver injury.
Arrange discharge if the first liver panel is normal and she remains asymptomatic.
explanations: At nine hours with a clearly toxic reported dose and delayed results, postponing antidote risks reduced benefit; early ALT can be normal.
Charcoal is not an antidote and is unlikely to be adequate as sole therapy this late after a standard immediate-release ingestion.
Correct. Start acetylcysteine when a potentially toxic ingestion is beyond eight hours and the level is not promptly available; reassess using concentration, timing and ALT.
Vitamin K may address selected coagulation problems but cannot prevent paracetamol hepatotoxicity.
Early normal liver tests do not exclude later hepatic injury; intentional overdose also needs psychosocial assessment.
pearl: For a potentially toxic late paracetamol presentation, do not wait for delayed concentrations before starting acetylcysteine.
pivot: A reliably timed early ingestion with a level available before eight hours can follow nomogram-directed treatment.

steps: Recognise
Assess timing, preparation, co-ingestants, weight and mental health safety.
Assess
Take paracetamol level, ALT, INR, glucose and renal tests.
Act
Begin IV acetylcysteine and consult toxicology if indicated.
Reassess
Review levels and enzymes before stopping antidote and arrange psychosocial care.
management.safety: Use the correct ingestion time and formulation; modified-release and staggered ingestions need different pathways.
management.local: Use current Australian clinical guidance, local protocols and senior support.

context: Original final-year Monash-style decision; inspired by 2024–2025 SPA-W review themes
stem: An 81-year-old who was cognitively independent before hip-fracture surgery becomes intermittently disorientated on postoperative day two. At night she tries to remove her cannula, but by morning she is calm. She has new urinary retention, mild hypoxaemia and has received several opioid doses. Her family asks for a sedative every night.
ask: What is the best initial management approach?
options: Prescribe regular benzodiazepines to prevent further nighttime confusion in all circumstances.
Diagnose irreversible dementia because she is elderly and has new memory difficulties.
Restrain her routinely overnight to protect cannulas without reviewing precipitating factors.
Assess and treat delirium precipitants while providing reorientation and supportive care.
Discharge immediately because fluctuating behaviour is expected after anaesthesia in older adults.
explanations: Benzodiazepines may worsen delirium and are not routine treatment unless specific indications such as withdrawal exist.
The abrupt fluctuating course with inattention suggests delirium, not necessarily a chronic neurodegenerative condition.
Restraint can increase distress and injury; use the least restrictive safe approach and address underlying causes.
Correct. Evaluate hypoxia, retention, infection, pain, constipation, medication effects and dehydration; involve family, sensory aids and nonpharmacological strategies.
Delirium predicts complications and warrants assessment and observation, not automatic discharge.
pearl: Delirium is acute and fluctuating; look for reversible medical, medication and environmental contributors.
pivot: Persistent dangerous agitation despite non-drug measures may justify carefully supervised short-term medication after risk assessment.

steps: Recognise
Screen attention and cognition and ask family about baseline.
Assess
Check oxygenation, bladder, bowel, infection, analgesics and metabolic status.
Act
Treat precipitants and use reorientation, sleep, mobility and sensory supports.
Reassess
Monitor falls risk and cognition, communicating recovery plan to carers.
management.safety: Do not use antipsychotics or sedatives routinely solely to make a delirious patient quiet.
management.local: Use current Australian clinical guidance, local protocols and senior support.

context: Original final-year Monash-style decision; inspired by 2024–2025 SPA-W review themes
stem: Immediately after a vaginal birth, a 30-year-old begins bleeding heavily. The placenta appears complete, her pulse rises to 120/min and the uterine fundus is enlarged and boggy. The birth team has called for emergency assistance and commenced haemorrhage resuscitation. There is no obvious genital tract tear.
ask: Which action most directly addresses the likely source of bleeding?
options: Observe for ten minutes because uterine bleeding usually settles after placental delivery.
Start a routine oral iron prescription before assessing uterine tone or blood loss.
Transfer to ultrasound first to exclude retained tissue before uterine massage.
Give prophylactic oral antibiotics alone because infection is the likely acute mechanism.
Perform uterine massage and give oxytocin promptly as part of the haemorrhage response.
explanations: Heavy ongoing bleeding with shock signs is not normal lochia and requires immediate intervention.
Iron replaces losses later but cannot control acute haemorrhage or restore uterine contraction.
Retained tissue remains a consideration, but a boggy uterus needs immediate atony management while evaluation proceeds.
Acute atony is mechanical failure of contraction rather than primary infection; antibiotics do not restore tone.
Correct. Uterine atony is the most common cause of primary postpartum haemorrhage; massage and uterotonics including oxytocin are early treatment alongside resuscitation.
pearl: A boggy enlarged uterus with postpartum bleeding strongly suggests atony; act on uterine tone immediately.
pivot: If the uterus is firm yet bleeding continues, examine for genital tract trauma, retained tissue or coagulopathy.

steps: Recognise
Activate PPH protocol, quantify bleeding and assess ABCs.
Assess
Palpate tone, inspect placenta and examine for trauma or retained tissue.
Act
Massage uterus, give oxytocin and support circulation with blood products as indicated.
Reassess
Escalate to compression, additional uterotonics, TXA and procedural control if bleeding persists.
management.safety: Do not delay blood-product resuscitation or escalation while repeating ineffective uterine massage.
management.local: Use current Australian clinical guidance, local protocols and senior support.

context: Original final-year Monash-style decision; inspired by 2024–2025 SPA-W review themes
stem: A 62-year-old with hypertension reports 45 minutes of crushing central chest pain radiating to the jaw. ECG shows new anterior ST depression; she is alert with BP 138/82 mmHg and no active bleeding. She has never had an aspirin allergy and has not received any medications for this episode.
ask: Which treatment should be administered promptly while definitive ACS assessment proceeds?
options: Give a chewable loading dose of aspirin unless contraindicated, alongside the ACS pathway.
Delay all antiplatelet therapy until the second troponin has confirmed myocardial necrosis.
Give thrombolysis immediately because any ischaemic ST-segment change indicates STEMI.
Give high-dose intravenous heparin alone without aspirin or diagnostic reassessment.
Start a prophylactic oral antibiotic because myocardial injury may reflect an infection.
explanations: Correct. Early aspirin reduces platelet aggregation and is standard initial treatment for suspected ACS when there is no contraindication; continue ECG/troponin and risk assessment.
A high clinical suspicion of ACS warrants aspirin before repeat troponin confirmation, barring bleeding or allergy.
ST depression suggests ischaemia but is not a standard STEMI fibrinolysis indication; evaluate the full ECG and clinical context.
Anticoagulation may be indicated after assessment, but it does not replace aspirin and should follow an appropriate pathway.
Antibiotics do not treat plaque rupture or coronary thrombosis; there is no evidence of infection.
pearl: Early chewable aspirin is appropriate for suspected ACS unless allergy or major bleeding risk prohibits it.
pivot: If aortic dissection is strongly suspected, reassess before antithrombotics because bleeding consequences may be catastrophic.

steps: Recognise
Assess ABCs, obtain 12-lead ECG promptly and review haemodynamics.
Assess
Give aspirin loading dose when not contraindicated and obtain serial troponin.
Act
Apply risk-based ACS therapy and seek cardiology input for invasive evaluation.
Reassess
Monitor pain, rhythm and bleeding while updating the diagnosis.
management.safety: Do not give nitrates to hypotensive patients or those with relevant phosphodiesterase inhibitor exposure.
management.local: Use current Australian clinical guidance, local protocols and senior support.

context: Original final-year Monash-style decision; inspired by 2024–2025 SPA-W review themes
stem: A 60-year-old develops sudden maximal-intensity chest pain tearing through to the back while lifting a heavy box. He has a new pulse deficit in the left arm and systolic BP differs by 35 mmHg between arms. ECG shows no ST elevation, and a colleague proposes treating presumed ACS with full-dose anticoagulation.
ask: What is the best immediate diagnostic strategy in this stable patient?
options: Administer therapeutic heparin first and request CT only if serial troponins become positive.
Arrange urgent CT angiography of the aorta with vascular or cardiothoracic escalation.
Use a D-dimer alone to exclude dissection because the ECG lacks diagnostic changes.
Perform exercise stress testing to reproduce the chest pain before specialist referral.
Discharge after analgesia if the first troponin and portable chest X-ray are normal.
explanations: Heparin may worsen bleeding in dissection and should not be started blindly when classic dissection red flags are present.
Correct. Abrupt tearing pain with pulse/BP asymmetry raises acute aortic syndrome; urgent CTA defines anatomy in a stable patient and prompts surgical planning.
D-dimer can contribute only in selected low-probability pathways and cannot replace imaging in a high-suspicion case.
Stress testing is unsafe in possible acute aortic pathology and is not a diagnostic test for dissection.
Normal early troponin or chest radiograph cannot exclude aortic dissection and do not justify discharge.
pearl: Pulse deficit plus abrupt tearing pain is aortic dissection until urgently excluded; antithrombotics may be harmful.
pivot: Unstable patients may need immediate bedside echocardiography and operative consultation rather than transport to CT.

steps: Recognise
Assess haemodynamics, limb pulses and neurological signs.
Assess
Obtain urgent CTA when stable and seek immediate specialist advice.
Act
Provide controlled analgesia and specialist-directed heart-rate/BP management.
Reassess
Monitor for tamponade, malperfusion and need for emergency surgery.
management.safety: Do not allow a normal ECG or chest X-ray to reassure you against a high-risk dissection.
management.local: Use current Australian clinical guidance, local protocols and senior support.

skill: Child head injury / deterioration during observation
context: Original final-year Monash-style decision; inspired by 2024–2025 SPA-W review themes
stem: A seven-year-old falls from a scooter and initially has GCS 15 without focal deficits. After two hours of emergency-department observation he becomes progressively sleepy, repeatedly vomits and now has GCS 13. His pupils are equal, but he is slower to follow commands than at triage.
ask: What is the safest immediate management?
options: Continue the existing observation schedule because equal pupils exclude intracranial bleeding.
Provide an antiemetic and discharge if vomiting settles before the next assessment.
Arrange urgent senior review and neuroimaging with resuscitation readiness.
Reassure the parents that drowsiness is a normal consequence of mild concussion.
Defer reassessment until the next day because the initial GCS was fully normal.
explanations: A fall in GCS is a high-risk sign even with equal pupils; routine observation without escalation is unsafe.
Symptom treatment cannot substitute for investigating deterioration in conscious state.
Correct. GCS decline of two points with repeated vomiting demands immediate senior review, consideration of CT and preparedness for neurological resuscitation.
Concussion is possible but cannot be assumed when consciousness worsens after a head injury.
An initially normal examination does not rule out evolving intracranial injury; delays risk irreversible deterioration.
pearl: A drop of at least two GCS points during observation is an emergency red flag after paediatric head injury.
pivot: A well child with isolated vomiting and otherwise normal examination may be observed rather than immediately scanned.

steps: Recognise
Repeat ABCDE and document serial GCS, pupils and limb power.
Assess
Call senior emergency/neurosurgical help and arrange urgent CT as indicated.
Act
Support airway and circulation and treat raised intracranial pressure if suspected.
Reassess
Reassess frequently and communicate deterioration to caregivers.
management.safety: Do not discharge a child whose consciousness or neurological examination has worsened.
management.local: Use current Australian clinical guidance, local protocols and senior support.

context: Original final-year Monash-style decision; inspired by 2024–2025 SPA-W review themes
stem: A woman breastfeeding a four-week-old infant develops a painful red wedge on one breast after several days of oversupply. She has mild malaise, temperature 37.7°C and no palpable fluctuance. She has been aggressively massaging the area and pumping after every feed to 'empty' the breast, which seems to increase swelling.
ask: Which advice is most appropriate now?
options: Stop all breastfeeding on the affected side until the redness has completely disappeared.
Use deep massage and extra pumping after each feed to forcibly clear the obstructed duct.
Start antibiotics in every case immediately and avoid all non-drug measures.
Continue feeding to the baby's cues, use cold packs and avoid vigorous massage or over-pumping.
Arrange emergency surgical drainage because any red breast segment indicates an abscess.
explanations: Continuing breastfeeding is usually safe and abrupt cessation may worsen engorgement and inflammation.
Aggressive massage and unnecessary extra milk removal can aggravate oedema and perpetuate oversupply.
Early inflammatory mastitis may improve with anti-inflammatory care; antibiotics are for suspected bacterial disease or persistent/worsening symptoms.
Correct. Current Australian advice supports on-demand feeds, anti-inflammatory measures and avoidance of deep massage and excessive pumping.
A breast abscess generally presents with a focal collection or fluctuance and requires assessment; redness alone is not an indication for drainage.
pearl: Treat inflammatory mastitis by reducing inflammation, not by aggressively 'emptying' the breast.
pivot: Persistent fever, worsening erythema or failure to improve within about a day should prompt bacterial mastitis assessment.

steps: Recognise
Assess systemic symptoms, breast findings and infant feeding.
Assess
Check for abscess signs, oversupply and ineffective latch.
Act
Recommend cue-based feeding, cold packs, rest and appropriate analgesia.
Reassess
Reassess within 12–24 hours and prescribe antibiotics if bacterial mastitis is suspected.
management.safety: Sepsis or suspected abscess requires urgent assessment; avoid vigorous breast massage.
management.local: Use current Australian clinical guidance, local protocols and senior support.

skill: Active suicidal plan / safe immediate disposition
context: Original final-year Monash-style decision; inspired by 2024–2025 SPA-W review themes
stem: A 27-year-old attends the emergency department after telling a friend she intends to overdose on tablets at home tonight. She has already collected several packs of medication and describes the timing and dose she plans to use. She appears calm, denies intoxication and asks to leave because she has work in the morning.
ask: What is the safest immediate response?
options: Accept discharge because a calm presentation makes an imminent attempt less likely.
Arrange routine outpatient counselling without assessing access to medications.
Ask a friend to check by text tomorrow while allowing the patient to leave alone.
Provide a generic crisis leaflet and discharge once the patient promises to stay safe.
Ensure immediate safety and urgent mental health assessment, with supervised care as indicated.
explanations: Calm behaviour does not negate a specific plan, access to means or near-term intent; discharge without assessment is unsafe.
Outpatient care may follow stabilisation, but imminent intent requires immediate structured assessment and safety measures.
A next-day text is insufficient protection when the patient has both a concrete plan and means available.
A verbal promise or leaflet is not a reliable substitute for assessing risk, supervision and restricting lethal means.
Correct. Specific imminent intent and access to tablets require a safe environment, assessment of capacity and legal options, urgent specialist review and collaborative means restriction.
pearl: Risk assessment prioritises intent, plan, means, previous behaviour and protective factors—not outward calmness.
pivot: A patient without current intent or means may still require a collaborative safety plan and rapid follow-up after assessment.

steps: Recognise
Ensure immediate physical safety, observation and removal of accessible means.
Assess
Assess intent, plan, means, psychiatric symptoms, supports and capacity.
Act
Involve the emergency mental health team and arrange appropriate safe disposition.
Reassess
Create a collaborative safety plan, follow-up and supported handover after stabilisation.
management.safety: Do not rely on a 'no-suicide contract' or apparent calm to discharge a patient with imminent intent.
management.local: Use current Australian clinical guidance, local protocols and senior support.
